extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / wartime U.S. public
extracted.subtask_description: Newspaper reporting of World War II military developments and domestic wartime policies (rationing, quotas, government directives) intended for a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sugar rationing rule
rubrics_metrics.description: One pound every five weeks will be allowed for every person who was 15 or older when sugar rationing started last May.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This works out to slightly more than one cup a day; sugar ration books were issued for everyone from babies to grownups, but only books where the age of the user appears as 15 or older can be used to get coffee. There will be no curtailment of sugar rations and new books will be available when the sugar and coffee stamps are exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sugar ration book for coffee
rubrics_metrics.description: The sugar ration book will be used for coffee and no new registration will be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The last 10 stamps in the book will be used for coffee; stamp numbering determines which stamp is good for which coffee ration (example: No. 27 will be good for the first coffee ration). Retail sales of coffee will be stopped at midnight Nov. 21 in advance of rationing which starts Nov. 29.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coffee rationing start and retail suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Coffee rationing starts Nov. 29; retail sales of coffee will be stopped at midnight Nov. 21 in preparation for rationing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details on restaurant rationing to be announced; substitutes (tea, cocoa, etc.) are not being rationed for the present and may be consumed without limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restaurant coffee rationing policy (anticipated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial users (restaurants) will be restricted to a certain percentage of their former consumption for coffee when rationing is implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details of the rationing for restaurants were still to be announced but it probably will follow that of sugar, restricting commercial users to a certain percentage of their former consumption. Patrons may substitute tea, cocoa or other beverages without limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Price Administration (OPA) pricing allowance for alcoholic beverages
rubrics_metrics.description: Dealers could raise their prices sufficiently to pass on government-imposed higher taxes on liquor, wines and beer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dealers could raise prices on drinks of straight liquor and on bottled beer but not on draft beer, per OPA guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tire quotas for November
rubrics_metrics.description: The OPA announced a quota of 1,090,206 recapped tires or re-capping services for the nation in November.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compared with the October quota of 939,940. Quotas for Grade 2 tires available to war workers were increased while reductions were made in quotas of new tires available for other drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cocoa / chocolate production limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplies of cocoa and powdered chocolate are being cut to 60 percent of the 1941 consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits domestic chocolate availability; cocoa bean grinding and other processing will be reduced accordingly because of supply and shipping uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility rules for supplemental 'C' gasoline rations tightened
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rules for supplemental 'C' gasoline rations will be tightened when nationwide rationing starts Nov. 22, with all salesmen eliminated from this class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change narrows the class of people eligible for supplemental 'C' rations; implementation date tied to start of nationwide rationing.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB style and production restrictions for enameled household ware
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Production Board (WPB) laid down rigid style and production restrictions for enameled household ware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restrictions are intended to conserve materials and redirect production to war needs; specifics of the style/production limits were issued by WPB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial scrap / salvage directive (WPB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial concerns must 'dig deeper' to uncover every possible bit of industrial scrap; large deliveries of industrial scrap are essential to production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WPB urged firms to uncover scrap, discontinue work that cannot be repaired, and provide as much scrap as possible (target figures mentioned, e.g., to help provide 12,000,000 tons). The salvage drive’s results were cited as an example of effective cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective Service / manpower recommendations (Maj. Gen. Lewis B. Hershey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hershey recommended tighter control of crop planting, abolition of voluntary recruiting for the armed forces, and additional curbs on non-essential industries to combat man‑power shortage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He called for four steps: (1) Agriculture must decide what to grow next year; (2) stop voluntary recruiting for armed forces and civilian activities supporting the war when properly allocated; (3) industry must halt 'stealing of workers' and prejudice against hiring women; (4) reduce absenteeism. He also urged greater efficiency and longer hours where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien Property Custodian seizures of enemy-controlled assets
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alien Property Custodian announced seizure of American assets of the French dyestuff combine (associated with Germany's I. G. Farben) and the American assets of nine Japanese-owned companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizures cited specific companies and were presented as standard wartime exercise of authority to take control of enemy-controlled or enemy-interest assets in the U.S.; details of companies and subsequent congressional review were reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on supplemental consumer goods (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various consumer goods and industrial items are being rationed or restricted (examples given: sugar, coffee, tires, cocoa, nylon stockings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists government actions: nylon hose supply expected to be nearly exhausted by Christmas buying; restaurant and retail restrictions; shipping uncertainties may further limit supplies; agencies (WPB, OPA) issuing quotas and style/production limits to conserve resources for the war effort.
